source: Brit has no desire to be here at Elsinore; she seems deeply unhappy, as though something's weighing heavily upon her. Maybe it's time I got to know her better.

source: I saw Bernardo performing in town today, as Katherine. I never knew. We grew up together, and I never knew. This doesn't change my feelings towards Bernardo, however she or he chooses to live in the future—but for now, the Bernardos in other worlds would clearly prefer to keep this information private.

source: Bernardo is Catholic, and prays in the mornings sometimes. He's deeply private about his faith, especially in light of the recent burnings of churches around the country. His father was also a religious man.

source: Horatio is religious, but he isn't Catholic or Lutheran. He called himself a 'heathen,' and claimed to worship 'devas' and 'asuras.' I'm not sure what that means.

context.type: 资料、界面或未定位对白

source: Thanks to me, Irma's quest to kick up a regular game of cards has finally succeeded. I hope she doesn't get in too much trouble with Bernardo when he inevitably finds out.

context.type: 资料、界面或未定位对白

source: I learned that Irma had a daughter and a husband once. But that was a long time ago. The child died while she served as wet nurse for Gertrude. That must be why she feels such an incredible drive to protect her.

context.type: 资料、界面或未定位对白

source: Quince is a traveling player who occasionally comes to put on productions at Elsinore Castle. He writes and performs all of his own material, often on short notice. I recall he was rather close once with the late King Hamlet, and was a favorite performer of his.

context.type: 资料、界面或未定位对白

source: Quince is somehow stuck outside the flow of time, like me. He's offered me his assistance in solving my way out of my own quandary. I hope I can ask him about anything I might encounter.

context.type: 资料、界面或未定位对白

source: I see. Quince isn't just repeating time along with me. He also seems to have some small ability to alter the flow of events. But if that's true, then why doesn't he just... alter his way out? Is he here for my sake?

context.type: 资料、界面或未定位对白

source: When I found Quince in the gallery, he spoke in riddles. Something about the nature and structure of a tragic work. Of course I've read many of the great tragedies-- and it sometimes feels like I'm living one-- but what does all that have to do with my predicament?

context.type: 资料、界面或未定位对白

source: Marcellus has thirteen children, and grandchildren at that. I had no idea he was so-- er-- prolific. Then again, having to raise thirteen children would explain why nothing fazes him.

context.type: 资料、界面或未定位对白

source: I found King Hamlet's abandoned notes describing the end of his life. He was like me. But he gave up, and let madness consume him. He knew and understood everything that was happening around him-- his brother's plot against him, his wife turning from him-- and he couldn't stop it. Now he remains in Elsinore, neither alive nor fully dead. But why? Will that happen to me, too?

context.type: 资料、界面或未定位对白

source: King Hamlet appeared before me one final time. He told me that there will be no true ending, no right ending. There is no such thing as happiness. All that remains is my power to choose. He urged me to use it wisely. He said that whatever I do, I must use it. Not simply give up, as he did. And... he called me... his friend.

source: My father was waiting, as usual, but not to chastise me -- rather, to invite me to some sort of feast in the Great Hall. I'll need to join everyone there.

source: Hrm. I should probably check on the meal.
This fire is—wahh! Hot! Hot! Too hot!
Look at you, Irma, dancing around like a village idiot!
Have some dignity!—But ooh, that pan...
Nothing but the walls and the chapel this way.
Father said Laertes was meeting with the King, did he not? He wouldn't be back there.
No one is on the walls right now. I should look somewhere else.
The King and Queen's private chambers are up that way. Laertes won't be up there.
Guard Captain Bernardo, give me your report.
Better give me the report again, Bernardo.
The Prince of Norway demands we surrender the north.
Surrender to Fortinbras? Hah! The balls of a stallion, that young prince!
Fortinbras claims the late King Hamlet, rest his soul, won those swamplands unjustly from his father.
My brother won them for Denmark, certainly, but with all the fairness afforded to war.
He can shed all the tears he likes for that swampland. I won't bother to hear his complaints.
Yes, my lord. We'll send our reply.
Dearest, what will we do if Fortinbras wages war on our lands regardless?
We'll fight him head-on. He's an impetuous young boy—no more threat than a gadfly to our throne, my love.
That's how my brother would have done it!
May he rest in peace.
Yes, yes, my brother's passed—but now is a time for Denmark's new glory. Now is the time for us to expand.
With my lovely Queen by my side, we will be a force far beyond anything the northern lands have seen before!
Prince Fortinbras will not retreat easily. He is hot-headed—as his father was. He has a temper, my lord.
Are you questioning my ability to provide for Denmark's battle plan when the time comes, Guard Captain Bernardo?
Not at all, my lord. Merely... suggesting.
My lord... I tire of this. And besides, I believe young Laertes must meet his father's beckon.
My wife is right. We've had enough of political affairs for now. Today is a day for celebration, after all!
Young Prince Fortinbras grows beyond his leash. We ought to engage not with him, but with his uncle, the true King of Norway.
Bernardo, have Voltimand deliver a message to the King with our terms.
At once, milord.
Now then. Laertes, Hamlet? Please come forward.
I've been given word that the both of you wish to have my formal permission to leave Denmark.
My King, I want to travel to Paris tomorrow morning, that I might learn about the breadth of life's offerings beyond Danish walls.
And I want to return to Wittenberg, because—I agree—these Danish walls are absolutely miserable.
I have some concerns about each of you. You are yet young men. Laertes, what does your father say?
He is worried, my King, but grants his blessing.
Then I must concede. Hamlet, on the other hand...
Your mother the Queen and I would prefer you near to us, Hamlet. You may not go back to Germany.
The funeral for my brother is two months past, and yet you still wear black!
I wear mourning attire while I still mourn my father.
The time for that has passed. You ought to think of me as your father now—your father the King. Nothing has changed.
For your own health, I desire that you stay in Denmark.
If that's your wish, Uncle.
As is customary, I have no choice. I never do.
Excellent! All is settled. And with that, let us break a little while. Court is dismissed.
Thank you, my lord! Thank you!
You are most welcome, Laertes. Swift travels, my boy!
Ophelia—whenever you are done here, come meet me outside. I've something I want to tell you before I meet with Father.
TEMP: You shouldn't see this! I am too busy to talk to anyone!
Ophelia! There you are, love.
And, as usual, doesn't even give me so much as a 'Hello, Father.'
Hello, Father.
That's better. And what are you doing all the way out here?
I wanted to be alone a while. It's quiet here.
Avoiding me, more like. Well, I've a small favor to ask of you.
Your brother's in the throne room, visiting the King about his voyage. But His Majesty tends to run overlong...
Won't you fetch Laertes for me? Tell him he's tardy. As usual, his trunks are sitting in his chambers, open and empty.
At this rate, he'll go to Paris with nothing but the clothes on his back!
That would come as no surprise to either of us.
Of course not.
Much as I try, I cannot help but think of how terribly I'll miss him.
And with all that's going on here in Denmark... war brewing, and such...
I think my hair has gotten a little whiter even as we stand here. The nerves are taking quite a toll on me.
Father, go and have a stroll. Breathe. I'll fetch Laertes.
This is why you're my favorite daughter.
Only daughter.
And that as well!
That meeting... we'd been in there an hour. You've freed me. Eternally grateful.
I sensed you needed rescuing, even though I know you've been waiting for a return to ordinary affairs.
It's refreshing, no? After the dark cloud that's descended on Elsinore lately...
The last few months certainly have been odd.
What was it you wanted to discuss, then?
You know, Ophelia... I'm going to miss you.
And I you, brother.
You and Prince Hamlet... you're not... anymore...?
Hamlet and I aren't... together anymore, Laertes. I swear it on Mother's grave.
Has he given you any trouble?
No. He's far more focused on glaring daggers at his Uncle Claudius.
How long has it been since his father's funeral? A month? Two? And yet he scarcely seems to have recovered.
King Hamlet could do no wrong in his son's eyes, I'm certain. No doubt Hamlet's grief has been overwhelming as of late.
And Hamlet hates his uncle for marrying his mother. I see the way he looks at him. His eyes...
Like a kicked dog, angry, fuming, unpredictable.
It is both proper and customary that Gertrude married her husband's brother after her husband's death. I've no idea why Hamlet's in a fit about it.
It has me worried he might take out his anger upon you.
Laertes. You needn't throw shoes any more.
Throw shoes?
You remember when we were small, that one summer when that baroness and her children came to visit Elsinore?
You mean those horrible little boys who pushed you down?
Yes. And when one of them pulled my hair and said it looked odd--
Ah. Right. I'd forgotten. I threw my boot at him.
And you've been doing it ever since.
No one pushes my sister around. Well, unless it's me, of course.
They won't. That's what I'm telling you. I can fend for myself now. I promise.
I'm not that little girl anymore. And I'm not going to let anyone do harm to me.
I suppose that's true, isn't it?
You really have changed.
I see something of Mother in you, now. She could be fierce like that.
